lessons.title: Noticing the Phenomenon & Building the Need: What Tool Is Missing?

quiz.prompt: A student stands 40 m from the base of a straight transmission tower and estimates that the angle up to the top is about 50°. The class tries to find the height using only algebra and Pythagoras. Which statement best explains why they get stuck?
choices: Pythagoras needs two sides of a right-angled triangle, but here only one side (40 m) and an angle are known.
Pythagoras can be used directly because 40 m and 50° are both known.
The tower does not form a right-angled triangle, so no method could ever work.
Pythagoras only works for triangles taller than 40 m.
quiz.rationale: Pythagoras links sides to sides, so it needs two known sides. Only one side and one angle are given, so students need a new tool that links an angle to side lengths.
quiz.placement: Predict: groups' 'best attempt' using only algebra and Pythagoras on the mini-whiteboard

quiz.prompt: A wheelchair ramp forms a right-angled triangle with the level ground and a vertical wall. The ramp is the sloping side. You stand at the angle where the ramp meets the ground. Which side is the ADJACENT side to that angle?
quiz.rationale: The adjacent side lies next to the marked angle and is not the hypotenuse. Here it is the ground. The ramp is the hypotenuse and the wall is the opposite side.
quiz.placement: Part A: Environment Scan (Triangle Hunt, labelling O, A and H)

quiz.prompt: In Part B, a group draws a right-angled triangle with a 40° angle. They measure the opposite side as 3.9 cm, the adjacent side as 4.6 cm and the hypotenuse as 6.0 cm. What is O ÷ H to two decimal places?
quiz.rationale: O ÷ H = 3.9 ÷ 6.0 = 0.65. The value 0.77 is A ÷ H, 0.85 is O ÷ A, and 1.54 is H ÷ O (the ratio upside down).
quiz.placement: Part B: Ratio Discovery Activity (computing O÷H, A÷H, O÷A)

quiz.prompt: A group draws three right-angled triangles that all have a 40° angle. Their hypotenuses are about 6 cm, 9 cm and 12 cm. They find O ÷ H = 0.64, 0.65 and 0.64. What does this result show?
choices: The O ÷ H values are almost the same even though the triangles are different sizes.
O ÷ H is always equal to the length of the hypotenuse.
O ÷ H gets bigger as the triangle gets bigger.
The group must have measured wrongly, because different triangles should give very different values.
quiz.rationale: The three values differ only by a tiny amount, which is measurement error. The data show the ratio stays nearly constant for the same 40° angle, although the triangle sizes differ.
quiz.placement: Part B: Ratio Discovery Activity (group table and 'circle any pattern')

quiz.prompt: In the mast problem, the right angle is at the base of the mast. The observer stands 40 m from the base, and the angle from the observer up to the top is 50°. The height is the side opposite the 50° angle, and the 40 m is the side adjacent to it. Which equation connects the height to the 40 m?
quiz.rationale: Opposite ÷ adjacent is the tangent ratio, so height ÷ 40 = tan 50°. Sine uses the hypotenuse and cosine uses the adjacent over the hypotenuse, and neither fits here.
quiz.placement: Explain: returning to the mast problem and writing 'height ÷ 40 = tan 50°'

quiz.prompt: Which of these is the best question to post on the Driving Question Board for the mast problem?
choices: Why do we have to do trigonometry?
How can we find the value of tan 50° without measuring a huge triangle?
quiz.rationale: A good question is specific and linked to the phenomenon. It names what is still missing (the value of the tan 50° ratio) and points to the next steps in the unit. The other questions are vague or not investigable.
quiz.placement: DQB: writing one question about the mast problem or the ratios

quiz.prompt: When drawing a model of the mast scenario (a vertical mast standing on level ground, with the observer 40 m away), where should the right angle be marked?
choices: At the top of the mast
At the observer's feet, where the 50° angle is
At the base of the mast, where the vertical mast meets the level ground
quiz.rationale: The mast stands straight up from the level ground, so the right angle is at its base. The 50° angle is at the observer's position.
quiz.placement: Model: initial annotated pencil sketch of the mast scenario

lessons.title: Defining Sine, Cosine, and Tangent — Naming the Ratios That Unlock the Mast

quiz.prompt: A student stands 40 m from the base of a mast and measures the angle from the ground up to the top as 50°. The mast's height is the side opposite the 50° angle, and the 40 m is the side adjacent to it. Which ratio links the angle to the height?
quiz.rationale: The height (opposite) and the 40 m distance (adjacent) are both involved and the hypotenuse is not, so the tangent ratio, opposite ÷ adjacent, is the one that links them.
quiz.placement: Predict: which side-ratio connects the 50° angle to the mast's height (Nakuru mast, 40 m from the base)

quiz.prompt: In a right-angled triangle PQR, the right angle is at Q and PR is the longest side. Looking from angle P, a learner labels side QR as 'opposite'. She then switches to look from angle R. What is side QR called now?
choices: Still opposite, because the side does not move
Adjacent, because it now lies next to the reference angle R
It has no label, because it is only labelled from angle P
Hypotenuse, because it is a side of the triangle
quiz.rationale: Opposite and adjacent depend on the reference angle. From angle R, side QR touches the angle and is not the hypotenuse, so it is adjacent.
quiz.placement: Observe: pairs label O, A, H for each acute angle in their two triangles, noticing that labels change when the reference angle switches

quiz.prompt: Two learners draw a right-angled triangle with an angle of about 35°. They measure the opposite side as 5.8 cm and the hypotenuse as 10.0 cm, so their sin 35° is 0.58. The mathematical table gives sin 35° = 0.574. What best explains the small difference?
choices: Small errors in drawing and measuring the sides; the table value is the reliable one
The table is wrong because it does not match their triangle
Their triangle is too small, so the sine ratio changes with size
They should have used adjacent ÷ hypotenuse for sine
quiz.rationale: Sine depends only on the angle, not the triangle's size. The small gap comes from measurement error with ruler and protractor, while the table value is pre-computed and accurate.
quiz.placement: Observe: learners open the sine table and compare table values with their computed ratios

quiz.prompt: A 10 m ladder leans against a wall and makes an angle of 60° with the ground. The ladder is the hypotenuse, and the height it reaches up the wall is the side opposite the 60° angle. Which ratio should be used to find that height?
quiz.rationale: The known side is the hypotenuse and the wanted side is the opposite, so SOH (sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse) is the ratio to use. Tangent would need the adjacent side, which is not given.
quiz.placement: Explain: SOH-CAH-TOA definitions and choosing the correct ratio

quiz.prompt: A student stands 40 m from the base of a mast and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 50°. From tables, tan 50° ≈ 1.192. What is the height of the mast, to 1 decimal place?
quiz.rationale: tan 50° = height ÷ 40, so height = 40 × tan 50° = 40 × 1.192 ≈ 47.7 m. Dividing gives 33.6 m, and using sin or cos gives the other wrong values.
quiz.placement: Explain: guided mast example, height = 40 × tan 50°

quiz.prompt: A surveyor in Kisumu stands 25 m from the base of a tree and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 38°. Using tan 38° ≈ 0.781, what is the height of the tree, to 1 decimal place?
quiz.rationale: tan 38° = height ÷ 25, so height = 25 × 0.781 ≈ 19.5 m. Dividing 25 by 0.781 gives 32.0 m, which is a common error.
quiz.placement: Explain: independent practice (a), the Kisumu tree problem

quiz.prompt: You know that sin θ = 0.643 for an acute angle θ and want to find θ using mathematical tables. What should you do?
choices: Divide 0.643 by 90 to get the angle
Find 0.643 in the sine table and read the angle that goes with it
Find 0.643 in the cosine table and read the angle that goes with it
Multiply 0.643 by 100 to get the angle in degrees
quiz.rationale: Tables list each angle with its sine value, so you can work backwards by finding the given ratio in the sine column and reading the angle. Here it gives about 40°.
quiz.placement: Explain: independent practice (b), back-calculating θ from sin θ = 0.643

quiz.prompt: You are adding ratio formulas to your right-angled triangle model, which has sides labelled opposite (O), adjacent (A) and hypotenuse (H) relative to angle θ. Which formula belongs next to the adjacent side and the hypotenuse?
quiz.rationale: Cosine is adjacent ÷ hypotenuse (CAH), so cos θ = A ÷ H goes with the adjacent side and the hypotenuse.
quiz.placement: Model: adding sin θ, cos θ and tan θ formulas to the Lesson 1 triangle model

lessons.title: Sines and Cosines of Complementary Angles: sin θ = cos(90° − θ)

quiz.prompt: Using mathematical tables, a pair finds that sin 25° = 0.4226. Which of these must also be equal to 0.4226?
quiz.rationale: 25° and 65° add up to 90°, so they are complementary and sin 25° = cos(90° − 25°) = cos 65°. The others are different ratios or different angles.
quiz.placement: Observe: complementary angle pairs table (25°/65° row)

quiz.prompt: Which pair of angles is complementary, so that the sine of one angle equals the cosine of the other?
quiz.rationale: Complementary angles add to 90°, and 42° + 48° = 90°. The other pairs add to 180° or 100°, so they are not complementary.
quiz.placement: Observe: class inspection of the completed master table

quiz.prompt: In a right-angled triangle ABC, the right angle is at C, angle A = θ and angle B = 90° − θ. Side a is opposite angle A, side b is opposite angle B, and side c is the hypotenuse. Which ratio equals sin(90° − θ)?
quiz.rationale: From corner B, the opposite side is b, so sin(90° − θ) = b/c. This is the same ratio as cos θ, because b is adjacent to angle A.
quiz.placement: Explain: right-angled triangle labelled from both corner A and corner B

quiz.prompt: Which of these is equal to cos 70°?
quiz.rationale: cos 70° = sin(90° − 70°) = sin 20°. Writing sin 70° ignores the change to the complementary angle.
quiz.placement: Explain: Practice set (A) Simplify: express cos 70° as a sine

quiz.prompt: Given that sin(2θ + 10°) = cos(θ + 20°), what is the value of θ?
quiz.rationale: The angles must be complementary, so (2θ + 10°) + (θ + 20°) = 90°. This gives 3θ + 30° = 90°, so 3θ = 60° and θ = 20°.
quiz.placement: Explain: Practice set (B) Solve for θ: sin(2θ + 10°) = cos(θ + 20°)

quiz.prompt: Which statement about sine and cosine of complementary angles is correct?
quiz.rationale: sin θ = cos(90° − θ), so sin 65° = cos 25°. The relationship swaps sine and cosine; it does not keep the same ratio for both angles.
quiz.placement: DQB: 'I now understand that…' statements and the WHAT WE NOW KNOW column

quiz.prompt: A mast stands on level ground. From a point 40 m from its base, the angle of elevation to the top is 50°. In the right-angled triangle formed, the angle at the top of the mast is 40°. Why can an engineer use either the 50° angle or the 40° angle to work out the mast height?
choices: Because sin 50° = sin 40° in the same triangle
Because the tangent of 50° and the tangent of 40° are equal
Because the two angles are complementary, so the sine of one equals the cosine of the other and both give the same triangle relationships
quiz.rationale: The two acute angles add up to 90°, so they are complementary. This means sin 50° = cos 40° and cos 50° = sin 40°, so either angle describes the same triangle.
quiz.placement: Model: annotating the Nakuru mast diagram with the complementary angle at the top

lessons.title: The Hidden Link: Discovering tan θ = sin θ / cos θ

quiz.prompt: Learners divided sin θ by cos θ for θ = 20°, 30°, 40°, 50°, 60° and 70°, and compared each answer with the tan θ value in their table. Every row matched, apart from tiny rounding differences. What is the best conclusion from this pattern?
choices: sin θ ÷ cos θ is never equal to tan θ, but the values are close
sin θ ÷ cos θ is sometimes equal to tan θ, depending on the angle
sin θ ÷ cos θ is equal to tan θ for every acute angle tested, so it looks like an identity
sin θ ÷ cos θ is equal to cos θ ÷ sin θ for these angles
quiz.rationale: All six rows agreed, which suggests sin θ ÷ cos θ = tan θ is always true for acute angles. The lesson then proves this algebraically.
quiz.placement: Observe: adding the 'sin θ ÷ cos θ' fourth column and comparing it with the tan θ column

quiz.prompt: In a right-angled triangle, sin θ = O/H and cos θ = A/H, where O is the opposite side, A the adjacent side and H the hypotenuse. What is (O/H) ÷ (A/H) after simplifying?
quiz.rationale: (O/H) ÷ (A/H) = (O/H) × (H/A). The H cancels, leaving O/A, which is the definition of tan θ.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher's board proof of tan θ = sin θ / cos θ

quiz.prompt: A Kenya Power engineer's calculator has a broken tan button. Her notebook says sin 50° = 0.766 and cos 50° = 0.643. Using tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ, what is tan 50° to 3 decimal places?
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem C, finding tan 50° from sin 50° and cos 50°

quiz.prompt: The angle of elevation to the top of a mast is 50°, and the horizontal distance from the observer to the base is 40 m. Using tan 50° = sin 50° ÷ cos 50° = 0.766 ÷ 0.643 and height = tan θ × horizontal distance, what is the height of the mast to 1 decimal place?
quiz.rationale: Height = 40 × (0.766 ÷ 0.643) = 40 × 1.1913 ≈ 47.7 m. Multiplying 40 by sin alone, or by cos alone, or dividing 40 by tan, gives the wrong answers.
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem C, computing the Nakuru mast height with distance 40 m

quiz.prompt: θ is an acute angle in a right-angled triangle and sin θ = 3/5. Without a calculator, what are cos θ and tan θ?
quiz.rationale: With opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5, the adjacent side is 4 (3-4-5 triangle), so cos θ = 4/5. Then tan θ = (3/5) ÷ (4/5) = 3/4.
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem A, given sin θ = 3/5, find cos θ and tan θ

quiz.prompt: For an angle of 35°, tan 35° = 0.700 and cos 35° = 0.819. Using tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ, what is sin 35° to 3 decimal places?
quiz.rationale: Rearranging tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ gives sin θ = tan θ × cos θ = 0.700 × 0.819 ≈ 0.573.
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem B, given tan 35° and cos 35°, find sin 35°

quiz.prompt: A mast is 95.4 m tall, and an observer stands 40 m from its base. Using tan θ = height ÷ distance, what is tan θ for the angle of elevation θ to the top?
quiz.rationale: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent = height ÷ distance = 95.4 ÷ 40 = 2.385. Dividing distance by height gives the inverted value 0.419.
quiz.placement: Model Building: extension task on a mast twice as tall at the same distance

lessons.title: Trigonometric Ratios of Special Angles (45°, 30°, 60°, 0°, and 90°)

quiz.prompt: In Construction A, a group draws an isosceles right-angled triangle with both legs (AB and AC) 6 cm long. What is the exact length of the hypotenuse BC?
quiz.rationale: By Pythagoras, BC² = 6² + 6² = 72, so BC = √72 = 6√2 ≈ 8.49 cm. Adding the legs (12 cm) is the common error.
quiz.placement: Construction A: isosceles right-angled triangle with legs of 6 cm, measuring BC

quiz.prompt: In Construction B, a group draws an equilateral triangle PQR with side 8 cm and bisects it by drawing PM perpendicular to QR, where M is the midpoint of QR. What is the exact length of PM?
quiz.rationale: QM = 4 cm and QP = 8 cm, so PM² = 8² − 4² = 48 and PM = √48 = 4√3 ≈ 6.93 cm. This is longer than QM but shorter than QP.
quiz.placement: Construction B: equilateral triangle of side 8 cm bisected into a 30-60-90 triangle, measuring PM

quiz.prompt: An isosceles right-angled triangle has both legs 1 unit long and a hypotenuse of √2 units. What is the exact value of sin 45°?
quiz.rationale: sin 45° = opposite/hypotenuse = 1/√2. Choosing √2 comes from inverting the ratio, and 1 is the value of tan 45°, not sin 45°.
quiz.placement: Part A: Exact derivation for the 45° triangle (legs = 1 unit, hypotenuse = √2)

quiz.prompt: A 30-60-90 triangle has sides 1 (opposite 30°), √3 (opposite 60°) and 2 (the hypotenuse). What is the exact value of tan 30°?
quiz.rationale: tan 30° = opposite/adjacent = 1/√3. Using √3 mixes up the sides, which gives tan 60°. √3/2 is sin 60°, and 1/2 is sin 30°.
quiz.placement: Part A: Exact derivation for the 30-60-90 triangle (short leg = 1, long leg = √3, hypotenuse = 2)

quiz.prompt: A surveyor in Nakuru stands 40 m from the base of a Kenya Power mast and measures the angle of elevation to the top as exactly 60°. Using tan 60° = √3, what is the height of the mast?
quiz.rationale: height = 40 × tan 60° = 40 × √3 = 40√3 ≈ 69.3 m. Dividing by √3 comes from wrongly using tan 60° = 1/√3.
quiz.placement: Part B: Mast application (angle of elevation 60°, distance 40 m)

quiz.prompt: Why is tan 90° described as undefined?
choices: tan 90° = 1, because the opposite side and the hypotenuse become equal
tan 90° = 0, because the adjacent side becomes 0
The adjacent side approaches 0, and division by zero is not possible
The opposite side becomes 0, so there is nothing to divide
quiz.rationale: tan θ = opposite/adjacent. As the angle approaches 90°, the adjacent side approaches 0, and dividing by 0 has no answer, so tan 90° is undefined.
quiz.placement: Part A: looking back at the trig-table columns to complete the values for 0° and 90°

quiz.prompt: After today's lesson, a group asks: 'Can we find the exact height of the Nakuru mast if the angle of elevation is 50°?' Which answer is correct?
choices: No, a mast can only be measured when the angle is 30°, 45° or 60°
Yes, use the 60° triangle, because 50° is close to 60°, and the answer will be exact
The two special triangles give exact values only for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, so for 50° we use tables or a calculator
Yes, use the 45° triangle, because 50° is close to 45°, and the answer will be exact
quiz.rationale: Exact surd values come only from the special triangles. For a non-special angle such as 50°, we use tables or a calculator, which gives an approximate value.
quiz.placement: DQB phase: blue sticky note new question 'What if the angle is 50° — can we get an exact answer, or must we use tables?'

lessons.title: Solving Right-Angled Triangles Using Trigonometric Ratios

quiz.prompt: A ramp at Kisumu County Referral Hospital makes a 12° angle with the ground. The horizontal distance along the ground is 6 m. You want the length of the ramp surface. Which ratio should you use?
choices: Cosine, because the known side is adjacent to 12° and the ramp is the hypotenuse
Sine, because the ramp is the side opposite the 12° angle
Tangent, because the ground distance is the side opposite the 12° angle
Tangent, because a ramp is a slope
quiz.rationale: The 6 m ground distance is adjacent to the 12° angle and the ramp surface is the hypotenuse. Adjacent and hypotenuse means CAH, so cosine is used.
quiz.placement: Predict: Diagram A, the Kisumu County Referral Hospital ramp (choosing the ratio)

quiz.prompt: A telecom mast in Garissa is 45 m tall and stands at a right angle to the ground. A support wire is anchored on the ground 45 m from the base of the mast. What angle does the wire make with the ground?
quiz.rationale: The known sides are opposite (45 m) and adjacent (45 m), so tan θ = 45/45 = 1. The angle whose tangent is 1 is 45°, a special angle.
quiz.placement: Predict: Diagram C, the Garissa telecom mast support wire

quiz.prompt: A student stands 40 m from the base of the Nakuru transmission mast. The angle of elevation to the top is 50°. Using tan 50° ≈ 1.1918, what is the height of the mast?
quiz.rationale: The known side (40 m) is adjacent and the height is opposite, so tan 50° = height/40. Then height = 40 × 1.1918 ≈ 47.7 m.
quiz.placement: Observe: worked example 'WORKED EXAMPLE — Nakuru Mast'

quiz.prompt: A ramp makes a 12° angle with the ground. The horizontal distance along the ground is 6 m. Using cos 12° ≈ 0.9781, what is the length of the ramp surface, to 2 decimal places?
quiz.rationale: cos 12° = adjacent/hypotenuse = 6/ramp, so ramp = 6 ÷ 0.9781 ≈ 6.13 m. Multiplying by cos 12° is a rearrangement error and gives a value shorter than 6 m, which is impossible for a hypotenuse.
quiz.placement: Observe: second demonstration, the Kisumu ramp co-constructed with the teacher

quiz.prompt: A ramp at Mombasa port makes a 15° angle with the horizontal. The ramp is 8 m long. What is the vertical height the ramp rises, to 2 decimal places?
quiz.rationale: The height is opposite 15° and the ramp is the hypotenuse, so sin 15° = height/8. Height = 8 × sin 15° ≈ 8 × 0.2588 ≈ 2.07 m.
quiz.placement: Explain: pair work, Problem 1 (Mombasa port ramp)

quiz.prompt: A surveyor in Garissa measures that a telecom tower casts a shadow 32 m long on flat ground when the sun's angle of elevation is 62°. What is the height of the tower, to 1 decimal place?
quiz.rationale: The shadow (32 m) is adjacent to 62° and the tower height is opposite, so tan 62° = height/32. Height = 32 × 1.8807 ≈ 60.2 m.
quiz.placement: Explain: pair work, Problem 3 (Garissa tower shadow) and the link back to the Nakuru mast

quiz.prompt: After solving a right-angled triangle, a learner writes: 'I know one acute angle and one side. Now I can find the other two sides and the other angle.' What does 'solving a right-angled triangle completely' mean?
choices: Finding every unknown side and angle from one known side and one acute angle
Finding the height of the triangle only
Finding the three ratios sin, cos and tan for the 90° angle
quiz.rationale: Solving completely means finding all unknown sides and angles. With one side and one acute angle, the ratios give the other sides, and the angle sum of 180° gives the remaining angle.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: 'What does solving a right-angled triangle completely mean — and can we now do it?'

quiz.prompt: For a named acute angle in a right-angled triangle, you know the length of the side opposite it and you want the length of the hypotenuse. Which rule from SOH-CAH-TOA should you use?
choices: SOH, because it uses opposite and hypotenuse
CAH, because it uses the adjacent side
TOA, because it uses the opposite side
TOA, because tangent is the ratio to use whenever an angle is given
quiz.rationale: Opposite and hypotenuse are involved, so SOH applies: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse. Tangent only links opposite and adjacent.
quiz.placement: Model: writing the decision rule box (SOH if O and H, CAH if A and H, TOA if O and A)

lessons.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression: Solving Real Height-and-Distance Problems Across Kenya

quiz.prompt: A student stands 40 m from the base of a mast and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 50°. Let h be the height of the mast in metres. The 40 m side is next to the 50° angle, and h is opposite it. Which equation should be used to find h?
quiz.rationale: The known side (40 m) is adjacent to the angle and the unknown height is opposite it. The ratio that links opposite and adjacent is tangent, so tan(50°) = h/40.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on the Nakuru mast (40 m, about 50°)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes an angle of depression?
choices: The angle measured downward from the horizontal to the line of sight
The angle between the ground and the observer's feet
The angle measured between the line of sight and the vertical line through the observer
The angle measured upward from the horizontal to the line of sight
quiz.rationale: An angle of depression is measured downward from the observer's horizontal line to the line of sight to an object below. The upward version is the angle of elevation.
quiz.placement: Part A: Diagram Construction (elevation and depression diagrams)

quiz.prompt: A person stands at the top of the Fort Jesus cliff in Mombasa, 20 m above sea level. The angle of depression to a dhow at sea level is 35°. What is the horizontal distance from the base of the cliff to the dhow, to 1 decimal place?
quiz.rationale: The cliff height (20 m) is opposite the 35° angle and the distance d is adjacent. tan(35°) = 20/d, so d = 20 ÷ tan(35°) = 20 ÷ 0.7002 ≈ 28.6 m.
quiz.placement: Part B: Worked Demonstration (Fort Jesus cliff depression example, 20 m and 35°)

quiz.prompt: A visitor at Uhuru Park, Nairobi stands 15 m from the base of a flagpole. The angle of elevation to the top of the flagpole is 62°. What is the height of the flagpole, to 1 decimal place?
quiz.rationale: The distance of 15 m is adjacent and the height is opposite, so h = 15 × tan(62°) = 15 × 1.8807 ≈ 28.2 m.
quiz.placement: Problem 1 (Elevation — Nairobi): flagpole in Uhuru Park

quiz.prompt: A surveyor in Kisumu stands 42 m (horizontal distance) from a five-storey building. The angle of elevation to the top of the building is 38°. What is the height of the building, to 1 decimal place?
quiz.rationale: The 42 m is adjacent to the angle and the height is opposite, so h = 42 × tan(38°) = 42 × 0.7813 ≈ 32.8 m.
quiz.placement: Problem 2 (Elevation — Kisumu): surveyor and five-storey building

quiz.prompt: A tourist stands at the top of a cliff 27 m above sea level. She sees a dhow at sea level at an angle of depression of 41°. Let d be the horizontal distance from the base of the cliff to the dhow. Which working correctly finds d?
quiz.rationale: The cliff height (27 m) is opposite the 41° angle and d is adjacent. tan(41°) = 27/d, so d = 27 ÷ tan(41°) = 27 ÷ 0.8693 ≈ 31.1 m. Writing tan(41°) = d/27 is the common error.
quiz.placement: Problem 3 (Depression — Mombasa): tourist at Fort Jesus cliff and dhow

quiz.prompt: From the top of a cliff, the angle of depression to a boat on the sea is 41°. What is the angle of elevation from the boat to the person at the top of the cliff?
quiz.rationale: The horizontal line at the cliff top and the horizontal line at sea level are parallel. Alternate interior angles are equal, so the angle of elevation from the boat equals the angle of depression from the cliff top, which is 41°.
quiz.placement: Cumulative right-triangle model: depression inset labelled 'Angle of Depression = Angle of Elevation (alternate interior angles)'

lessons.title: Synthesis, Real-Life Applications, and DQB Review — Solving the Nakuru Mast at Last

quiz.prompt: A student stands 40 m from the base of a mast and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 50°. The 40 m side is adjacent to the 50° angle, and the height of the mast is the opposite side. Which ratio should be used to find the height?
choices: Pythagoras' theorem only, since 40 m is a known side
quiz.rationale: The known side is adjacent and the unknown side is opposite, and tangent links opposite and adjacent. Sine and cosine involve the hypotenuse, which is not known, and Pythagoras needs two sides.
quiz.placement: Predict Phase: writing the Nakuru mast calculation tan 50° = height ÷ 40 m before class sharing

quiz.prompt: A mast stands on level ground. From a point 40 m from its base, the angle of elevation to the top is 50°. Given that tan 50° ≈ 1.1918, what is the height of the mast to the nearest 0.1 m?
quiz.rationale: tan 50° = h ÷ 40, so h = 40 × tan 50° ≈ 40 × 1.1918 ≈ 47.7 m. Dividing by tan 50° gives 33.6 m, which is a rearrangement error.
quiz.placement: Observe Phase: STEP 4 — Solve, h = 40 × tan 50° for the Nakuru mast

quiz.prompt: In the right-angled triangle for the mast problem, the observer's foot is at the 50° angle. The mast is vertical, the ground distance to the mast is 40 m, and the observer looks along a line of sight to the top of the mast. Which statement correctly names the sides relative to the 50° angle?
choices: The 40 m ground distance is the hypotenuse, and the line of sight is adjacent
The 40 m ground distance is adjacent, the mast height is opposite, and the line of sight is the hypotenuse
The 40 m ground distance is opposite, and the mast height is adjacent
The line of sight is opposite, and the mast height is the hypotenuse
quiz.rationale: Relative to the 50° angle, the side touching the angle along the ground is adjacent and the side across from it (the mast) is opposite. The line of sight is the longest side, the hypotenuse, and it is not needed in this problem.
quiz.placement: Observe Phase: STEP 2 — Identify known and unknown sides relative to the 50° angle

quiz.prompt: A fisherman in a boat on Lake Victoria looks up at the top of a lighthouse and measures the angle of elevation as 30°. A coastguard at the top of the lighthouse looks down at the same boat. Assuming the water level is horizontal, what is the angle of depression from the coastguard to the boat?
quiz.rationale: The horizontal line at the top of the lighthouse and the water level are parallel, so the angle of depression equals the angle of elevation (alternate angles). 60° is the complementary angle, which is a common mix-up.
quiz.placement: Explain Phase: Lake Victoria lighthouse task, drawing the angles of elevation and depression correctly

quiz.prompt: A boat on Lake Victoria is 120 m from the base of a vertical cliff. The angle of elevation of the cliff top from the boat is 38°. Given that tan 38° ≈ 0.7813, what is the height of the cliff above the water to the nearest 0.1 m?
quiz.rationale: The 120 m side is adjacent and the height is opposite, so tan 38° = h ÷ 120. Then h = 120 × 0.7813 ≈ 93.8 m. Dividing 120 by 0.7813 gives 153.6 m, which is the wrong rearrangement.
quiz.placement: Explain Phase: Lake Victoria problem, mark scheme step (a) h₁ = 120 × tan 38°

quiz.prompt: While solving a two-triangle height problem, a learner subtracts two heights to find a cliff height and gets a negative answer. What is the best next step?
choices: Assume the calculator is faulty and guess the height
Redraw the diagram and check which angle belongs to which height, since a length cannot be negative
Switch to cosine for every part of the problem
Ignore the minus sign and give the answer as a positive number
quiz.rationale: A negative length is impossible, so it signals a set-up error. The lesson's message is that careful diagram work, checking which angle links to which side, fixes such errors.
quiz.placement: Explain Phase: the 'productive contradiction' discussion when the arithmetic 48.5 − 93.8 does not make sense

quiz.prompt: The unit driving question asks: 'How can we use the angles and one side of a right-angled triangle to find any unknown height or distance?' Which answer is best?
choices: Use only the tangent ratio in every problem, whatever sides are known
Measure the height directly by climbing with a ladder
Use Pythagoras' theorem, because it links angles to sides
Choose sine, cosine or tangent depending on which sides are known and unknown, then link the known angle and known side to the unknown side
quiz.rationale: Trigonometric ratios link an angle to a ratio of sides. The ratio chosen depends on the sides involved (SOH-CAH-TOA). Pythagoras relates sides only, and tangent is not the only ratio.
quiz.placement: DQB Review: answering the unit driving question card in one sentence

quiz.prompt: In their final model, a learner writes the complementary-angle relationship sin 35° = cos θ. What is the value of θ?
quiz.rationale: The relationship is sin θ = cos(90° − θ), so sin 35° = cos(90° − 35°) = cos 55°.
quiz.placement: Model Building Phase: annotating the Final Model with the complementary-angle relationship sin θ = cos(90° − θ)
